problem: Social navigation (find and follow a human) policies in Habitat 3.0 either need privileged information such as humanoid GPS at test time, or ignore human motion. Human trajectories are only partially observable from the robot's egocentric view and expensive to predict.
motivation: Human-robot collaboration such as search-and-rescue or elder care needs a robot that stays 1-2 m from a person and backs off when needed. Ground-truth human position is unavailable on a real robot, so the useful signal has to be recovered from what the robot can sense and do. The paper borrows RMA-style system identification for this.
key_idea: Train a policy in stage 1 conditioned on a latent encoding of privileged human trajectories, then in stage 2 train an adapter that regresses that latent from the robot's own state-action history, so no privileged information is needed at deployment.
insight: Which privileged signal is used matters a great deal: trajectories are better than humanoid GPS for adaptation. hGPS encodes the robot's own position, which is hard to regress, and it is corrupted when a wall separates the human from the robot; with hGPS adaptation S drops to 0.57-0.70 and ES to 0.02-0.03, versus 0.91 and 0.43 with trajectories. Trajectory length matters too: 20 steps is best, 1 step (plain RMA) gives ES 0.03, and 50 steps degrades. An MLP encoder beats a Transformer (ES 0.50 vs 0.12).
method: Stage 1 social policy: DD-PPO recurrent policy takes ResNet depth features, a humanoid-detection bounding box, the previous action, and a latent z_t = mu(human trajectory of 20 past x-y positions). mu is a 3-layer MLP with 128-d output, trained end-to-end with the standard PPO loss.

Stage 2 social dynamics adapter: an MLP psi with alternating spatial and temporal layers maps the history of robot states and actions to z_hat. It is trained with MSE against z_t while the frozen stage-1 policy runs on z_hat; everything else is frozen.
Deployment: the frozen policy runs on z_hat inferred from history only. There is no hGPS and no trajectory input, and the adapter can run at a lower update rate.
Baselines: a Habitat 3.0 DD-PPO baseline with hGPS, and the Cancelli et al. proximity tasks (risk and compass) adapted as auxiliary tasks.
Realism tests: ORCA for human avoidance, adapter update rates of 1/2 and 1/100, Redwood depth noise, Gaussian bounding-box and actuator noise, human speed changes, and multi-human scenes.

setting.backbone: DD-PPO recurrent policy + ResNet depth encoder + MLP trajectory encoder and adapter (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Habitat 3.0 social navigation episodes; stage 1 is 250M DD-PPO steps over 24 environments, stage 2 is 5M supervised steps; no extra data
setting.observation: egocentric arm and stereo depth + humanoid detector bounding box (no RGB used by the policy)
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity commands in the robot's local frame
setting.privileged: human trajectories during training only; none at test time for SDA-S2. The S1 and hGPS rows use GT privileged inputs at test time. The heuristic expert uses a map.

results: Without privileged information, SDA-S2 reaches S 0.91, SPS 0.45, F 0.39 and ES 0.43, against the Habitat 3.0 baseline's 0.76, 0.34, 0.29 and 0.40 and Baseline+Proximity's 0.85, 0.41, 0.37 and 0.41. Its collision rate is higher (0.57 vs 0.48) because it follows the human for longer. The gap to the baseline persists under noise, lower update rates and multi-human scenes.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation; training relies on human trajectories that are not available in real deployments.
Higher collision rate than the baseline; failures come from constrained space, blind spots and not finding the human. Adaptation works with trajectories but not with hGPS.
The policy is trained with a single human at constant speed; performance drops in multi-human and variable-speed settings.
